title: Substitution
hook: the Reformers stressed Christ bearing the penalty in our place (Isaiah 53:5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, satisfaction: Anselm's ledger, a debt we owe and can't pay. Your line was he paid what we owed.

A prison door swings open in Jerusalem, and a man named Barabbas walks out into the daylight. Mark calls him a man held with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising. He was in chains. Then the Roman governor lets him go: Pilate "released Barabbas unto them, and delivered Jesus, when he had scourged him, to be crucified." One man walks free. Another goes to the cross. The Gospels never say what Barabbas did next, or whether he ever stood near Golgotha and looked up. But some readers have stood in his sandals ever since.

Substitution means one in the place of another. Christians reading the cross this way go back to a song in Isaiah about a servant who suffers: "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." Notice the little words: for our, upon him. The wounds belong to one, the healing to others. The first letter of Peter picks up the song: Christ "his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree." Here's what's new since yesterday. Anselm said a wrong is made good or punished, and put the cross on the payment side. The Reformers, Luther and Calvin among them, stressed the other side: the penalty for sin was real, and Christ bore it, in our place. Paul says it sharply to the Corinthians: "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." Luther called this a happy exchange: Christ takes what is ours and gives us what is his. Some who hold this picture call it their peace: the verdict has already been carried. Other Christians hold it more lightly, or worry it can sound like a Father punishing an unwilling Son. Those who hold it close answer that Father and Son act as one, out of the same love: God himself carries the cost. Churches weigh it differently. At its heart is Barabbas, and the open door.

Picture the door open in front of you, daylight outside, and name one thing you carry that you can't put down by yourself: a wrong you did, a weight you can't fix. If you pray, thank God for bearing what you couldn't; if you don't, notice what it would be like to walk through that door with your hands empty.
Substitution. One in the place of another: Christ bearing the penalty of sin so that others go free.
Your line: in my place. The door is open, and Barabbas walks out. That's today, done.

howItsDone: In Reformed, Lutheran and evangelical churches, sermons, hymns and communion prayers speak of Christ dying in the believer's place, and some churches read Isaiah 53 during Holy Week.

chat.says: What does substitution stress that Anselm's payment picture didn't?
options: The penalty itself: the Reformers stressed that Christ bore the punishment for sin in our place.
That Barabbas offered to die for Jesus, so the story really runs the other way round.
That Isaiah's song of the suffering servant is about Barabbas, not about the cross.
chat.meaning: Anselm put the cross on the payment side. The Reformers, Luther and Calvin among them, stressed that the penalty was real and Christ bore it in our place.

Barabbas.meaning: the prisoner Pilate released while Jesus was sent to the cross

Pilate.meaning: the Roman governor who handed Jesus over to be crucified

Golgotha.meaning: the place where Jesus was crucified

notes: Barabbas appears in Matthew 27, Mark 15, Luke 23 and John 18; the script says only 'the Gospels tell this moment' under the claims rule.

Mark 15:7 paraphrased: Barabbas 'lay bound with them that had made insurrection with him, who had committed murder in the insurrection'. The script says 'held with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising'. Confirm.
The hook avoids naming the crowd's role to keep Rome's responsibility clear; Pilate releases and delivers. Confirm this is fair to the Gospel accounts.
